findings.title: GET request mutates user state, bypassing CSRF protection
findings.body: The new `unsubscribe` action is wired to two GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) but it mutates state (changes `TopicUser#notification_level` and calls `save!`). Rails only checks CSRF tokens for non-GET requests, so any third-party page, image, link prefetch, or email preview that causes a logged-in user to issue a GET to these URLs will silently change that user's notification level. By contrast the existing `set_notifications` endpoint in this same controller correctly uses `post`. This new action must be POST/DELETE (or use a signed one-time token) and use Rails' `protect_from_forgery`/`verify_authenticity_token` flow.

findings.title: `ensure_logged_in` makes the email unsubscribe link unusable
findings.body: The whole point of this feature is the link the user receives in a notification email. The new `:unsubscribe` action is added to the `before_filter :ensure_logged_in` list and the route is a plain GET, so any recipient who clicks the unsubscribe link from their mail client without an active Discourse session is bounced to the login page instead of being unsubscribed. Standard email one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058) requires an authenticated-by-token flow; here the URL must carry a per-user, per-topic signed secret that authorises the notification change without requiring a login.

findings.title: `NoMethodError` 500 when the user has no `TopicUser` row
findings.body: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` returns `nil` whenever the recipient of the email has never actually visited the topic (for example they were only `@mentioned` or quoted). The very next line does `tu.notification_level > ...`, which raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass` and the user gets a 500 page in place of the intended unsubscribe. The action must handle the no-row case (e.g. via `TopicUser.change`, which already creates the row when missing), or at minimum guard the comparison.

findings.title: Toggle logic downgrades watching/tracking only to `regular`, so the user keeps getting emails
findings.body: The branch `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` sets the level to `:regular` (which still sends notifications) for users who were `:watching` or `:tracking`. The only path that actually stops emails is the `else` branch (regular/muted -> muted). Users who were actively watching the topic and click 'unsubscribe' will continue receiving notification emails, which is the opposite of what the link promises. The action should mute (or apply the level chosen by the user via the page UI) rather than treat the operation as a `>= regular ? regular : muted` toggle.

findings.title: Bypassing `TopicUser.change` skips the `MessageBus` publish and reason tracking
findings.body: `TopicUser.change` is the existing canonical way to mutate a `TopicUser` row: it sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` when `notification_level` changes, publishes `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` so other tabs/clients update in real time, and creates the row when missing. This controller fetches the row, mutates the attribute, and calls `save!`, so (a) no `MessageBus` event is fired (open clients keep showing the old level), (b) `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not refreshed, and (c) any race where the row is deleted between `find_by` and `save!` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`. The action should delegate to `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`.

findings.title: Action renders the topic page instead of acknowledging the unsubscribe
findings.body: After mutating the notification level, the action falls through to `perform_show_response`, which renders the normal topic view. The user (who came from an email expecting a confirmation) is dropped on the regular topic page with no visible feedback that anything happened, and the URL they bookmark/share contains `/unsubscribe`. There is no redirect to a confirmation screen and no flash/notice. Either render a dedicated confirmation view or redirect to a stable page that reflects the new state.

findings.title: No tests cover the new per-topic unsubscribe URL in the email body
findings.body: The new `unsubscribe_link` server locale adds a `%{unsubscribe_url}` markdown link (`To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url})`), and `user_notifications.rb` now passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`. The updated spec only asserts that the existing `user_preferences_url` is present; there is no expectation that the new `unsubscribe_url` is actually rendered into the body, nor any test for `Topic#unsubscribe_url`, `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, or the `notification_level` change behaviour. Add a test that the body contains the topic unsubscribe URL and that `Topic#unsubscribe_url` returns the expected path.

findings.title: Typo `stopNotificiationsText` is misspelled
findings.body: The new controller property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (extra `i` before `ations`). It is referenced with the same spelling from `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` so it happens to work, but the name should be `stopNotificationsText`. Rename both occurrences to match the locale key (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`) and remove the future risk of someone 'fixing' only one side.

findings.title: `bottom: initial` is unlikely to do what was intended
findings.body: The new rule `.topic-unsubscribe .notification-options .dropdown-menu { bottom: initial; }` uses the CSS-wide keyword `initial`, resetting `bottom` to its initial value (i.e. `auto`). That just undoes any prior offset and is almost certainly not the intent — the goal was presumably to override the default dropdown placement for the embedded button on the unsubscribe page. Use an explicit value (`auto`, `100%`, or a measured offset) instead of `initial`, otherwise the rule is effectively a no-op.
